subject: biology
title: Osmosis and water potential
key_idea: **Osmosis** is the net movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, from a higher water potential to a lower water potential. It is passive. What it does to a cell depends on the solution around the cell.

blocks.text: This section covers what osmosis is and how water potential predicts which way water moves.

items.meaning: The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane.
A measure of the tendency of water molecules to move. Symbol ψ, measured in kilopascals (kPa).
A membrane that lets some molecules through, such as water, but not others, such as larger solutes.

items: Pure water has the highest water potential, which is 0 kPa.
Dissolved solutes lower the water potential, so solutions have negative values.
The more concentrated the solution, the more negative the water potential.
Water molecules are free to move, and they diffuse from high to low water potential across the membrane.
Water keeps moving until the water potential is equal on both sides, so there is no net movement.

blocks.text: Water molecules move in both directions. The net movement is towards the lower water potential, because more molecules are free to move from the side with the higher potential.

items: Osmosis is net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane.
Water moves from a higher to a lower water potential.
Pure water is 0 kPa, and solutes make the value more negative.

sections.heading: Osmosis in plant and animal cells

blocks.text: A cell placed in a solution gains, loses or keeps its water. Plant cells have a cell wall, and animal cells do not.

items.meaning: A plant cell full of water, pressing against its cell wall.
A plant cell that has lost so much water that the cell-surface membrane has pulled away from the cell wall.
An animal cell bursts after taking in too much water.

options.label: Plant cell in pure water
results: The cell becomes turgid. The cell wall stops it bursting.

options.label: Plant cell in a very concentrated solution
Plant cell in a solution of equal water potential
results: The cell stays the same size.

options.label: Animal cell in pure water
results: The cell swells and bursts, because there is no cell wall.

options.label: Animal cell in a very concentrated solution
results: The cell shrinks and the membrane becomes crinkled.

options.label: Animal cell in a solution of equal water potential

items: Turgid plant cells press against each other and support the plant. Cells that lose water cause wilting.
An animal cell has no wall, so in a solution of higher water potential it can burst.
Animal cells need surrounding fluid close to the cell's own water potential to stay the same shape.
Higher outside: cells gain water. A plant cell becomes turgid and an animal cell can burst.
Lower outside: cells lose water. A plant cell is plasmolysed and an animal cell shrinks.
The cell wall protects a plant cell from bursting.

blocks.text: Osmosis can be shown with non-living materials and with plant tissue.

items: Fill Visking (dialysis) tubing with a sucrose solution and place it in water. Visking tubing is partially permeable.
The tubing swells and gains mass as water enters. This shows that water moves towards the lower water potential.
Agar can be used in a similar way, with different concentrations of solution around it.

blocks.text: Estimating the water potential of plant tissue

items.text: Prepare a dilution series of sucrose solution, from pure water up to a concentrated solution.
Cut equal-sized pieces of potato and measure the mass of each.
Place one piece in each solution for the same time and temperature.
Blot dry and measure the mass again. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
Plot percentage change in mass against solution concentration or water potential.
Where the line crosses zero, there is no net movement of water. The tissue has the same water potential as that solution.

blocks.label: Percentage change in mass
blocks.formula: percentage change = (final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100

items: A gain in mass is positive and means the tissue gained water. A loss is negative.
Calculating the percentage lets pieces of different starting mass be compared.
Control tissue type, piece size, time, temperature and volume of solution.
Visking tubing swells when it is placed in a solution with a higher water potential.
The concentration where the percentage change is zero matches the tissue's water potential.
Percentage change in mass allows fair comparison.

checks.a: The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane.

checks.q: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated sucrose solution. Explain what happens to it.
checks.a: The solution has a lower water potential than the cell. Water leaves the cell by osmosis, so the cell loses volume and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall. The cell is plasmolysed.

checks.q: Pieces of potato are placed in sucrose solutions and their percentage change in mass is plotted. The line crosses zero at 0.3 mol/dm³. Explain what this shows.
checks.a: At 0.3 mol/dm³ there is no net gain or loss of water. The water potential of the potato tissue is equal to the water potential of that solution.
